rationale: The review describes mitochondrial dysfunction and cognitive impairment in Parkinson disease across clinical and model sources. It surveys disease processes and candidate approaches without a measured dried fig or visual hallucination episode outcome.

The insula imaging meta-analysis considers 96 reports and maps fMRI and PET comparisons. Visual hallucination groups appear in the source-study inventory, including Ballanger's receptor PET study. The imaging synthesis has no dietary comparison or pooled visual episode rate.

The Mayo autopsy cohort estimates cerebellar-predominant progressive supranuclear palsy frequency. An individual case records visual hallucinations during the clinical course. Autopsy diagnosis is PSP and the report offers no dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode count.

The review compares acetylcholine imaging approaches across dementia and parkinsonian disorders. Its clinical phenotype and receptor associations do not measure dried fig intake or episode frequency following a food exposure.

Seventy-two people across controls, Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies underwent EEG and MRI. The 21-person DLB group showed higher NPI hallucination scores than the Alzheimer group. The clinical item and diagnostic-imaging grouping address a different population and outcome from food-timed Parkinson visual episodes.

The authors describe an LRRK2 Arg1441Ser carrier with Parkinson disease and visual symptoms in the course of long-term care. Genetic phenotype, medication changes and a briefly recorded antipsychotic intervention provide case context. There is no dietary exposure or episode count.

The 167-person dementia with Lewy bodies cohort relates MRI hippocampal volume to survival. The authors report frequency of hallucinations as a sensitivity covariate, with no dedicated episode-rate estimate. The paper does not evaluate dried fig intake.

Resting-state fMRI compared 17 rigid, 15 tremor-predominant Parkinson participants and 24 controls. The experimental outcomes concern network connectivity and motor-subtype differences. No dried fig intake or clinical visual episode outcome is measured.

The review distinguishes waking hallucinations, dreams and experiences at sleep onset or awakening. Its comparison across Parkinson disease, eye disease and schizophrenia considers phenomenology and mechanisms. No original dried fig or Parkinson visual episode-frequency result is reported.

The review evaluates hearing impairment and auditory processing in dementia. It differentiates sensory impairment and auditory symptoms from other clinical presentations, with no exposure to dried figs or visual episode counting.

The 12-person Parkinson dementia or Lewy body dementia pilot compared two active nilotinib dose groups with open-label monitoring. It reports one mild hallucination event in the lower group and two in the higher group and describes broader psychotic symptoms during changes to other Parkinson medications. The event report does not classify visual modality or frequency, and the trial had no dried fig exposure.

The autopsy-correlated PET case series reports five people with Parkinson disease dementia. Four had a hallucination item marked present at imaging, and individual histories sometimes distinguish visual symptoms from sleep phenomena. Amyloid imaging and tissue measures do not test a food or clinical episode-frequency contrast.

The European multicenter cohort measures cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers among 375 participants with dementia with Lewy bodies, 55 with Parkinson dementia and 164 with Parkinson disease. Its outcomes concern biomarker-defined copathology and cognitive measures, without a dried fig or timed visual episode comparison.

The 12-volunteer visual-motion experiment uses dopamine-drug sessions and focal transcranial magnetic stimulation to compare discrimination under transient visual noise. The volunteers did not form a clinical Parkinson hallucination cohort. The task does not test dried figs or visual hallucination episodes.

A healthy volunteer pharmacological challenge compares resting-state network connectivity after serotonergic and cholinergic interventions. It mentions prior visual hallucination research in discussing potential mechanisms. The exposure and outcome do not match dried fig intake or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The dementia delirium review compares diagnostic signs, instruments and distinctions between attention or awareness change and chronic cognitive impairment. It describes clinical presentations without a dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode rate.

The international cohort checks C9orf72 repeat expansions in dementia with Lewy bodies and distinguishes neuropathological from clinical ascertainment. This genetic comparison does not test dried fig intake or visual episode frequency.

The review evaluates cardiac sympathetic MIBG imaging in Lewy body disease and related differential diagnoses. It addresses tracer uptake and standardization, without an original dried fig exposure or clinical visual episode-frequency contrast.

The Korean study enrolls 323 Parkinson patients and 94 controls. The K-NMSS perception problems and hallucination domain is a composite, reported in 23.8% of Parkinson participants and with higher scores in advanced disease. The domain cannot identify a separate visual episode rate or a dried fig effect.

The 119-person Parkinson imaging cohort classifies cognitive phenotypes. Table I reports presence and severity from MDS-UPDRS item 1.2. Most positive observations were illusions, unformed experiences or formed hallucinations with preserved insight. Prevalence and ordinal severity do not give a food-timed visual episode count.

This 2016 Todd and Teale guide describes delirium screening and clinical timing, including visual and auditory signs. A 2017 version has a distinct DOI and a substantially overlapping main body, without a new clinical cohort. Neither edition measures a dietary exposure or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The review considers sleep disturbances and their relationship to amyloid and other pathways in Alzheimer disease. Its sleep outcomes, amyloid context and references do not test dried figs or waking Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The review evaluates mixed neuropathology and implications for therapeutic development. It distinguishes visual hallucinations as a clinical feature of Lewy body dementia from postmortem diagnoses and comorbid tissue changes. It has no dried fig intake or symptom episode-rate comparison.

The viewpoint reviews Lewy body dementia psychosis evidence and quotes two caregiver reports from a 2009 association forum. The reports concern safety, general psychosis, functioning and treatment tradeoffs. They provide no measured dried fig exposure or separate visual episode rate.
